name: Torph
tagline: One animated text-morphing component for React, Vue and Svelte, MIT and with no runtime dependency
description:
Torph is a single component that morphs one string into another. Its own line: "Text continuity for interfaces on the web." The demo morphs "Processing Transaction" into "Running late, be there soon."

It ships for three frameworks from one package. The usage tabs show React, TypeScript, Vue and Svelte, and the peer dependencies name React 18, Vue 3 and Svelte 5.

The package carries no runtime dependency at all. It installs with `npm i torph` and the site gives the same line for pnpm, yarn and bun.

Lochie makes it. The repository lochie/torph sits at 1,157 stars under the MIT licence, and the last push was 7 September 2026. npm reports 252,168 downloads in the last month across 14 released versions.

The version is 0.1.3, so the API may still move.

The site carries a playground, examples and a showcase.
pricing_detail: Free and MIT. There is no paid tier.
agent_guidance:
Reach for this when a label changes in place and a hard swap reads as a glitch. A status line, a countdown, a streaming answer that settles.

Import from the framework entry, not the root. The site shows `import { TextMorph } from 'torph/react'`, and Vue and Svelte have their own entries.

It costs nothing in dependencies. The package declares no runtime dependency, and React, Vue and Svelte are peers.

Pin the version. It sits at 0.1.3, so treat the props as unstable and read the repository before an upgrade.

The site publishes no llms.txt and no sitemap. Read the README in lochie/torph for the props.
why_it_matters: A text morph is usually a bespoke animation or a whole motion runtime. This is one MIT component with no runtime dependency that works the same in React, Vue and Svelte.
tier_reason: 1,157 stars, MIT, no runtime dependency, three frameworks from one package, and 252,168 downloads in the last month with a push on the day of checking. Held below S because it is one component at version 0.1.3, and the site publishes no llms.txt, no sitemap and no written prop reference.

name: Libraries.dev
tagline: Five MIT React effect libraries built for coding agents, each shipping a copy-paste prompt, at about 2M npm downloads a month
description:
Libraries.dev publishes five React effect libraries and points them at coding agents. Its own heading: "High-crafted UI libraries for AI agents."

The five, with their npm names: Beam is border-beam, a rainbow glow riding the border of any element. Orb is thinking-orbs, thought-orb loading states for AI interfaces. Gooey is liquid-gooey, pieces that merge and morph like goo. Metal is metal-fx, a liquid-metal WebGL ring around buttons and icons. Image is img-fx, a WebGL image-generation loader for cards.

All five are MIT and free on npm. Each declares no runtime dependency, except img-fx which needs three as a peer. The site puts all five together at about 83 KB gzipped, and they need React 18 or newer.

The agent path is the point. Every library page carries a Copy prompt button that packs the install line, the usage and every prop into one paste for Claude Code, Cursor or Codex.

npm reports 1,999,426 downloads across the five in the last month. The site states "2,300,000+ installs".

Jakub Antalik makes it, with Alexandr Brinza on Orbs and Martin Petercak on Metal.

A Pro plan unlocks a Studio for deeper tuning, presets, and a skill for a coding agent.

pricing_detail: The five libraries are MIT and free on npm, and the site says they stay free. Pro is a separate plan for the Studio, the presets and the agent skill. Solo costs $9 a month, $90 a year, or $149 once. Team costs $39 a month, $390 a year, or $499 once. Pro adds a commercial licence for unlimited projects, client work included.
agent_guidance:
Install from npm by the package name, not the display name. The five are border-beam, thinking-orbs, liquid-gooey, metal-fx and img-fx. The site calls them Beam, Orb, Gooey, Metal and Image.

Use the Copy prompt button on a library page. It hands you the install line, the usage and the full prop vocabulary in one paste, which is faster and more exact than reading the playground.

Add three as a peer only for img-fx. The other four declare no runtime dependency at all.

Budget about 83 KB gzipped for all five, and React 18 or newer. The default theme is "auto", so light and dark resolve without a prop.

Do not trust a status code from this host. It has a catch-all route: /zzz-not-a-page returns 200, and /llms.txt and /sitemap.xml both return the HTML shell rather than a file. Real pages include /beam, /gooey, /metal, /image, /how-to-use, /studio and /pro.
why_it_matters: It is the clearest example of a component library designed around the agent rather than the reader: every effect ships as a prompt, and the paid tier sells a skill that teaches an agent the parameter vocabulary. Two million npm downloads a month say the approach works.
tier_reason: Five MIT libraries at 1,999,426 npm downloads in the last month, every one with no runtime dependency, a per-library copy-prompt for coding agents, live playgrounds and a stated bundle cost. Held below S because the site publishes no llms.txt and no sitemap, and a catch-all route returns 200 for any path, so an agent cannot tell a real page from a missing one.
